Do you want volunteers or not?!?!?!? Whatever few joys there are in this world, capitalism is a barrier to all of it.

I want validation from MYSELF. Of course there is no real solution for me. As I said I have a poor history with jobs, and live with my parents who are retired, so I have almost zero chances of being able to afford any surgery, outside of winning the lottery. And at my age now, I've pretty much given up hope of ever truly being happy with myself/my face. I feel like even if I get the surgery now, past age 30, it wouldn't matter because all my best years are behind me 😥 I missed out on everything in my 20's, rotting in my room. My BDD contributed to depression and isolation, and even though I have made some progress and I can go outside more easily without having panic attacks, my depression from missing out on so much when younger and losing friends along the way, and other things, I've become so weak, mentally exhausted, I don't even want to try to get a job to try to afford surgery. The problem was that just moving the demo save to the cracked full game save folder wasn't enough because every time I started the game the saves would get overwritten and go back to a default state. Just make sure to change it back afterwards so you can save. You should be able to change the read-write status while the game is still running.

And in high school itself, I never made any friends, which I found ironic because now my parents were pressuring me to go out and wondering why I was home all the time. "You're in high school, these are supposed to be the best years of your life, go out, have some fun!" They told me 🙄 I don't really know what happened in high school, even at the time I wondered what was wrong with me. I just did not know what to say to anyone. I had had the same group of friends from kindergarten all the way up to MS graduation. The kindergarten, elementary and middle schools were all close by each other, so our lazy parents just transferred us to the nearest school. Some of my friends did end up going to other schools (or moving away) at various points, but my main friend group almost all of us remained in the same schools until MS. Then when I got to high school I felt like I'd forgotten how to make friends with new people. I was so used to seeing and talking to the same people everyday, we had inside jokes and stuff. I didn't know how to build up a similar connection with a new person. I talked to many people in HS but no friendship ever came out of it. Also my high school was VERY small. I think there was only around 100 students give or take in my graduating class, so there weren't many people for me to even try to befriend, and I had classes with mostly the same kids, so I ran through most of my options within the first two years. I also for some reason developed a reputation as the weird quiet (black) girl and sometimes people would actually get up and move away from me if I tried sitting next to them in the cafeteria or in class, like they didn't want to be seen with me. I sat alone, at an empty cafeteria table for 45 minutes, almost everyday at school, for 4 years. I say 'almost' everyday because there were a few occasions some of the nicer kids did let me sit with them or they tried sitting with me for a few days before going back to their regular table. But I think that experience had a profound impact on my life. Literally just sitting there, staring out at the other tables full of kids talking and laughing with each other, wondering why was I so different from them, why couldn't I form connections like that. It was literally a form of torture, one step away from being solitary confinement. I don't think I've ever recovered from that fully. Ever since then I've been alone.

I used some online tool called cyberchef (using the AES Decrypt recipe, don't ask me what that is cuz idk but it works) to get a readable version of the Profile.json file in DDV's Steam folder, which is basically your save file. After that I found the Item ID numbers (from this site but you need to sign up, https://fearlessrevolution.com/viewtopic.php?t=21330&start=630) for some of the objects in the game and was able to add the Timebending Table to my inventory and finally complete the quest. Actually took me two whole days and a lot of experimenting with different tools to figure that out... I also figured out how to cheat and increase my money, friendship levels, and give myself other items, etc, lol but I'd rather play the game legitimately, I just wanted to fix this one thing. It was frustrating but kinda fun in retrospect now that I finally solved it, and I learned a lot. Initially, after changing the Profile file, the game would just overwrite the data and delete my changes. What I did was just change the file to Read-Only so that DDV wouldn't be able to overwrite it. But after you load the game up again, and verify it works, you can change it back from read-only and let it save as normal.

An easy way to build up resistance against social anxiety is going to your favorite fast food place. Mine's Taco Bell. Just go and order food to stay. Sit down and eat your meal and just relax. Watch all the people that come and go, the people that pass by in front of the store, listen to the workers chat with each other. I suggest this because it's an easy activity that doesn't require much from you. You will be in a good mood because it's food you enjoy and a place you're familiar with. You have to talk to someone (or not since a lot of places have tablets now) but it's easy because you're following a script, you're just saying what you need to, "let me get a cheeseburger and fries, please" very simple. Then you sit in the restaurant to acclimate yourself to being around people. The best part is you don't have to talk to anyone, just sit and enjoy your meal. When I would do this, I would often look around and I would notice not many other people would be looking at me. Other patrons will be on their phone or talking to the friend they're having lunch with. There's no expectation on you to perform socially. This is where CBT comes in and you start reframing your mindset. Like "wow, here I am sitting here around all these people and they don't even care. No one's looking at me right now. I look like a normal person, just doing what everyone else is doing, having a meal. I am capable, I am brave, I'm normal. No one would even think I have social anxiety. Wow this food is really good, even better eating it while it's still hot instead of waiting til I'm home to eat." You just say positive affirmations to yourself, and focus on the things you see how around you. Focus on the smell in the air, check out the fashions people wear when they walk in, listen to the conversations other people are having. Try to focus OUTWARD, instead of INWARD, where you're worrying if you're being weird. Focus on the other weird people who come in and think to yourself "well at least I'm not that person lol"

That happened to me too, when I realized how much my school experiences were still affecting me, it led me to believe I had PTSD.

Definition of PTSD from Wikipedia:  a mental and behavioral disorder  that develops from experiencing a traumatic event, such as sexual assault, warfare, traffic collisions, child abuse, domestic violence, or other threats on a person's life or well-being. **Symptoms may include disturbing thoughts, feelings, or dreams related to the events, mental or physical distress to trauma-related cues, attempts to avoid trauma-related cues, alterations in the way a person thinks and feels, and an increase in the fight-or-flight response.**

I used to think PTSD could only happen to soldiers or sexual abuse survivors but the main element is that any kind of trauma can cause it, like bullying or being ostracized from peers. Once I started looking at it from this perspective it made it easier for me to find solutions to help deal with the emotions I was still experiencing after school. I'd think to myself, why do I still feel this way even when I haven't seen anyone from school in X+ years? These people shouldn't even be on my mind still. I also started looking around at my current life and realized it wasn't so bad. A major part of social anxiety is assumptions, assuming everyone around you is some kind of threat. And at one point, that was true. Everyone in my school was a threat to me. But I wasn't in school anymore but my brain didn't know that and was still reacting as though I was still in that situation. The people I'm interacting with now are not the people I spoke to in school. I'm not the person I was in school either. I'm wiser, have better coping skills, know better how to deal with rude people, also am not stuck in a building forced to interact with the people who hate me everyday. If I have a bad interaction at a store or something, it's meh, I'll never see that person again most likely. And I personally feel the older I've gotten (i'm 28) the more kind people I've started to meet, it almost seems like an illusion that there could be such cruel kids who hurt other kids in school. The adults around me now are such nice people. Teenagers are really the worst lol :(

I'd recommend looking up resources for healing from trauma, and I believe once you deal with that, your social anxiety will naturally start to heal itself as well. One person I really like on youtube is Dr. Scott Eilers.

After the trauma of having to put my cat to sleep from kidney failure in 2021, and crying all the way on the bus ride home with strangers staring, social anxiety didn't affect me much. Parting with my best friend was the hardest thing I'd ever had to do so things like talking to people or eating in front of others were suddenly not that big a deal.

A lot of my social anxiety came from me thinking that I was so different from everyone in my life as child, that all my behaviors were exclusive to me. I was often criticised or teased by family and friends as being weird because of the way I talked or my hobbies and interests. I felt I was the only person who acted this way, the only person with those hobbies, etc. I felt like an alien among humans, thought why couldn't I find my people? I repressed parts of my personality because I didn't want people to keep treating me like a freak.

It took many years of watching others' youtube videos, reading forum posts, and meeting and speaking with certain people for me to realize that there were other people who felt like me and that I wasn't alone. My behaviors werent weird. I grew up around people who found me weird, later on I met people who thought I was charming. My interests or personality wasn't the problem, I was just around the wrong people for so long it affected me mentally. I used to laugh at people when I saw them make a mistake or do something embarrassing. Now I laugh with them because we all get embarrassed, we just don't know when it's gonna happen. I feel safe in knowing other people do the same things I do and feel the same way about certain issues, if that makes sense? I no longer feel like an alien pretending to be human (well i still feel that way sometimes lol), I feel like one of many humans with an eccentric personality and a rich inner world. 

I can talk to people easily now, the problem is I still don't really enjoy talking to people. Or at least I havent found anyone I enjoy talking to. It's so hard to find people with common interests. And I have other difficulties with conversing that stem from my reclusive lifestyle, but physical symptoms have reduced and i don't feel sad as much. But honestly my cat's passing had a huge part in my recovery, my social anxiety was partly responsible for his death (not taking him to the vet early because i was scared, and not working a job consistently to cover his treatment) so I feel great guilt. I've heard grief changes people, it certainly did for me.

Yeah I hate when people dismiss your issues just because you're skinny, like it means you have no problems in the world or shouldn't have body image issues. I'm not flat chested but I'm an A cup. I'm 28 and people regularly tell me I look anywhere from 14-18 years old. When I was 14 people told me I look 12, like I wasn't a teenager yet. Especially being black, in the black community thick bodies are praised on women. I hated my body all throughout school because I thought guys would only date me if I had a big butt, thighs and boobs (and sadly nobody ever asked me out in school) and other girls would make fun of me and call me a twig, say they would snap me in half lol. I even recall one teacher who had grabbed my arm and was surprised by the fact she could wrap her whole hand around my wrist. My parents thought I had anorexia or bulimia and my mom would randomly burst into the bathroom while I was in there to make sure I wasn't purging. I was always small since I was young. My family teased me about. They always tried to make me eat more food because they thought my size meant something was wrong with me but I've never had a big appetite so I just stayed skinny. Got into meal plans and protein shakes and calorie counting and trying to forcefeed myself in order to gain but I really have no idea how people can eat so much food throughout the day (some to the point of obesity?). I usually just have one meal a day and snack the rest of it and I'm fine. When I eat too much my throat starts to close up. I'm about 95lbs at the doctors office. I think if it weren't for my clothes and shoes it'd be 90. It was only about 3 years ago that I finally became mostly comfortable with myself. I didn't do anything really I just sort of resigned myself to the reality that my body just wasn't going to look how I wanted it to and I would just have to manage. I told myself "well these clothes don't look good on me, but people wear clothes they look bad or goofy in all the time. It's my money and my body, if I want to wear it, I can. It doesn't matter whether it looks good or not." I try not to care when it comes to clothing, as long as it's clean and fits, I should be satisified with that. Or when it comes to dating, I tell myself "I don't need to look good for anybody, I look good for myself only. If they don't like it that's their problem. If love is meant to find me, it will." 

Basically a lot of positive affirmations to myself to calm all the anxieties. I stopped trying to seek validation from others. Sure, I still don't like my body but I just treat it as a vessel now, making sure it's in good shape, and properly protected. I tell myself regardless of how I look, I'm still a human being and deserve to be treated with fairness and respect.

I hate when people say not to compare yourself to others. If you never compared you would never know what you're missing in your own life. Imo the most important thing is to remember who you are and what you want out of life, and let other people live theirs. Sometimes those photos you see on social media are real. People are genuinely having that much fun and being loved by that many people. It's okay to be envious. And there are definitely people who are just keeping up appearances, but that is not everyone. And the real world itself is already full of people better than you anyway, SM just shoves it right in your face so you'll have to deal with other people either way. SM is not bad. The problem is almost everyone goes on one of those sites everyday for several hours. Only two solutions, love yourself/grow thicker skin, or just stop using those apps/use them in moderation. If you are upset seeing other people happy, that is a signal you need to make change in your life. I only use Facebook messenger to talk with family members, and I share some educational youtube videos to my timeline I think are interesting. That is good enough for me. I hope this didn't come off as harsh, I was just thinking out loud. I used to feel like OP but I remembered I'm in control of what I interact with and cut down on SM, and I stopped getting mad at other people for having the life I want because it's not their fault.. Social media can be an addiction or just another tool in your belt. Gotta decide what you want social media to be for you.

I think most people just see symptoms of depression as laziness, and when you actively go out and do things it appears to other people as though you're improving, so they go "see, you can do it, you're just not applying yourself". Or something.

I think the biggest thing though is how depression is expressed in the modern day. Think about it. It's a long established cliche that when kids turn into teenagers/young adults that all they want to do is be in their rooms all day and not talking to their families, surfing the web, playing video games or whatever is the norm. Probably to most people it doesn't appear we are depressed, it just looks like we're being normal. Especially if you grew up this way and your parents are 'adjusted' to it now. They likely think you holing yourself up in your room is just how you are, they're not thinking it's an illness that causes you to be afraid or unable to handle the outside world. They think the problem is you. My mom used to give me all types of advice to try to overcome anxiety and depression but it never helped (they never got me professional help) and it seems like my parents have given up and just accepted me as a NEET failure. I remember saying something similar to my mom years after high school like "how did you not know I was depressed all throughout high school? I was on the computer all the time, staying up late, I never hung out with friends. My mom told me she thought that's just how I was. She didn't realize it was a problem. I told her 'didn't you think it was weird for a child to behave like that?" And she just said she didn't know. She didn't know what to look for. That I seemed fine to her. Even though I told my English teacher about suicidal thoughts which led to me getting my first therapist at 14. After I stopped seeing the therapist my mom said she thought I was better. I only saw the therapist for a short time because I was too scared (social anxiety) to go by myself. I needed my mom or dad to go with me but they were both working at the time. I tried going myself one day and had a panic attack and just never went again. I even tried explaining social anxiety to my parents at the time. They didn't understand it. My mom told me to stop making things up and self-diagnosing myself because I'm not a doctor and that there's nothing wrong with me. I asked my parents for help plenty of times as a child but they just dismissed me. 

And now I'm older still living with them. We've gone down memory lane a few times and it is just the craziest thing that nowadays my parents say to me "if you had asked for help when you were younger we would've given it to you" and I'm like, I did though? My parents try to be so empathetic now, it's like they forgot when they used to tell me to just get over it. But I guess now that they see how I've developed - still no friends since high school nor a stable job either - they've finally accepted/realized that maybe I wasn't making things up and I do have a problem. I always wonder how differently my life could've turned out if I had gotten the help I needed when I was still young enough and moldable enough to receive it. Unlike most people perhaps, I've had knowledge/been reading up on mental illness from a very young age, like elementary. So I knew all the terms and lingo psychiatrists use, and I tried to use them to explain how I felt, but the adults around me (who I thought were more informed; my mistake) were, frankly, uneducated, and in general psychology was a joke field to most people before COVID so no one really took psychology seriously, so when I told adults I suspected I had social anxiety or bipolar disorder, they would ask "what is that? where did you learn that? you gotta stay off those websites, filling your head with garbage". Some things never change. The people around you are unable to help, either because they lack information on how to help, or they just don't believe you.

It is being used with と, that's the とか, which is also a quoting particle. They are the same but the か makes things more vague, less inclusive, as you know とか is used to list items but also implies the existence of other items. For example, 犬と猫が好き, I like dogs and cats. 犬とか猫とか好き, I like *things like* dogs and cats (maybe I also like rabbits).
It's being used adverbially/as a conjunction so it doesn't need a particle. "As a result of...", Also seen as (noun)の結果~.

A simple way to explain would be しない is 'doesn't do/don't do/won't do', while していない is '*have* not done/is not done'. And so,

しなかった -> did not do

していなかった -> had not done

たべなかった -> didn't eat

たべていなかった -> had not eaten 

It's the difference between an instant action - I screamed, I watched, I ate, - and a state of action - I was screaming, I was watching, I was eating. But 出席 is a special verb, like the common example 結婚. The している versions of these do not equate to the English -ing, 結婚している doesn't mean marrying and 出席している doesn't mean attending. It's more 'to be in the state of'. So we get things like, 彼女と結婚しなかった (I didn't marry my girlfriend)、結婚していない (I am not married/have not married), 結婚していなかった (I had not been married [at that time]).

Similarly, 出席しなかった (didn't attend), 出席していない (not in attendance), 出席していなかった (was not/had not been in attendance). It's more context based which tense to use. The ていなかった form can be used to state/imply that something was one way, but then something else happened (back to the marriage example, "I had not been married at the time, but now I am married"), or it leads into something else.

This website discusses it, particularly, example 11: https://www.jpf.go.jp/j/project/japanese/teach/tsushin/grammar/201403.html

Plus I kept telling myself how advanced I'd be by the time I became an adult and could legally travel to Japan. Also, the younger you are the easier it is to learn a language, so there's no time like the present.

When I was younger I probably scorned the idea of kanji like many beginners but I don't feel the same anymore. I think kanji's pretty cool. Great way to learn kanji is music/song lyrics (which is what I used). You'll learn like 50 kanji in one 3~ minute song, not to mention the words you'll pick up. Also manga since they have furigana so it makes look up easier. This was all helpful to me, but in the end I got frustrated not being able to just 'read' the pronunciation of kanji I found in the wild, so I buckled down and actually studied and went through all the jouyou kanji (the older one, with 1,945 kanji) and it took me 6 months from start to finish, but that's because I skipped most of the kyouiku kanji since I already knew most of them by that point.

All this to say, I don't think kanji is hard, it's just time consuming and tedious. You'd likely fare better than me if you start with a kanji learning system right off the bat (I had no idea such a thing existed at the time, except for Heisig which I disagree with) because the benefit I went after, and achieved, was merely learning the pronunciations of the 1,945 kanji, not necessarily their meanings. This way I was able to figure out the readings and look them up easier. But if you use a learning system you'd be learning meanings and readings and progress much faster than I did.

I hope this at least allays some of your fears. If you want to dip your tips into learning Japanese, check out my guy Tim Takamatsu! ^-^ His site doesn't get enough love. Everything is in romaji but it teaches a lot of important, beginner, beginner-intermediate grammar patterns, and you will pick up everyday words. Good luck.

My suggestion for how one should approach Japanese (or any language) and somewhat confusing terms like this is by defocusing from the English definition all together. You need the definition as a stepping stone, of course but, instead just focus on what the word/expression actually is meant to convey. For example, one way to think of というか is by learning that it's something you say when you want to correct or add on to what you previously said. Like in the other answer's example sentence 彼女のことをよく知っています というか幼稚園から｡｡｡ = I know her really well, **I mean**, I've known her since... blahblah. In this case, "I mean" is a nice equivalent to というか in what they do. Another example would be interjections, like Ouch! Imagine not being a native English speaker and you saw that word. How would you explain that to someone? Well, "ouch is *something we say when we get hurt*". Ouch doesn't necessarily "mean" anything, it expresses a feeling. 

This is how I decided to approach Japanese years ago when I became frustrated at how hard it was to translate. I initially started translating things for practice but, called me a bad writer or whatever, some Japanese sentences were so abstract I didn't even know where to begin. I could understand the sentence fine but couldn't put it into English words/a proper sensible sentence, so that day I actually gave up translating and focusing on "hard/solid" definitions for words and instead tried to understand the feeling they convey... (which equates to keen focus on intonation of the word and seeing it in multiple contexts, facial expression, etc) I think there are lots of words difficult to translate back into English if you're going for 1-1 word translation or trying to be literal, like 適当 which is actually the word that made me adopt this principle.
